> One concern I have here is that, as I understand it, the module system doesn't cache the fetched resource, it caches the result of processing the fetched resource. This might be a mismatch here and/or require additional syntax to clarify the intent, at least in some cases. For example, assume here that an `importmap` exists for `"foo": "./foo.css"`:
> 
> @import url('./foo.css'); /* rule 0 */
> @import url('./foo.css'); /* rule 1 */
> @import url('speicifer:foo'); /* rule 2 */
> @import url('speicifer:foo'); /* rule 3 */
> In that sheet `rule[0].styleSheet !== rule[1].styleSheet`, and I believe that's not up for debate.
> 
> But does `rule[2].styleSheet === rule[3].styleSheet`? If they act like JS modules, then the answer is yes. I very much want this to be the case. Is that the intention here?

Yes, that is the intention here. The fact that it's not the case for URLs is unfortunate. Ideally, we'd want to solve this for URLs too, in a backwards compatible way. Basically, a behavior that URLs can opt-in to that does this, but specifier URLs have it by default. What would that look like? An HTTP header?

Related specifically to @import: https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/8297. Also mentioned in that issue is @jakearchibald's proposal for [fetch-maps](https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/8297#issuecomment-1521917534), which has at least some of the caching but via a separate namespace I think.

This is super interesting. A few questions/potential gotchas:

1. Existing imports currently go through the module map and use specifiers (without any sort of prefix). Does this proposal imply that a Javascript `import foo;` and `import specifier:foo;` are equivalent for script-based specifier imports, or is this proposal only targeted to HTML + CSS?
2. This is somewhat similar to `<base>`, and it might be helpful to list out differences or pro's/cons so it doesn't get confused or sidetracked. It also might help to describe how this is expected to work with `<base>` (I assume specifiers ignore `<base>`, but I'm not positive, it might still apply after import map resolution). 
3. Script execution has finer control over when script is executed vs parsed via `async` and `defer`, so it can wait until all content (including import maps) have been parsed before executing (if desired). HTML has no such constructs, so you could have:
```
<link rel="stylesheet" href="specifier:foo" id="first">
<script type="importmap">
{
  "imports": {
    "foo": "styles.css"
  }
}
</script>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="specifier:foo" id="second">
```

...and only the second `<link>` would have its bare specifier mapped via the import map. This is different than how resource fetching works in HTML, where the order of parsing the DOM doesn't impact URL resolution.

One possible solution to this kind of thing would be to introduce `async` or `defer`-like attributes for each of these, which won't scale everywhere (e.g. CSS `@import` doesn't take an attribute, so it would require updates to its grammar, and I would imagine there are other strange cases). Deferring the fetch could postpone the overall load time pretty significantly though, so maybe the ordering dependency is less bad?

4. With external CSS fetches via `<link rel="styleshet">` or `@import`, you could get race conditions like this:

```
<style>
@import(a.css)) /* this kicks of an async fetch of "a.css" */
</style>
```
(where `a.css` has `@import(specifier:foo)`)

Then you have:
```
<script type="importmap">
{
  "imports": {
    "foo": "styles.css"
  }
}
</script>
```

`a.css` gets fetched asynchronously, and parsing continues. The CSS `@import` fetching behavior is [somewhat vaguely spec'd](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade-5/#at-import), but the actual behavior in browser engines seems to be async fetches with a synchronous ordered insertion of imported rules once each fetch completes. The async fetch of `a.css` means that fetching `specifier:foo` could fail, as it would be racing with the import map parsing. 

One option is to defer these types of fetches until parsing is complete as suggested in 3). Waiting to fetch resources until parsing completes is bad, and this would also break optimizations like the [speculative parser](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#active-speculative-html-parser). This case seems worse than the ordering dependency in 3), as it's non-deterministic.

> maybe the ordering dependency is less bad?

That seems fine to me and is, I think, de facto what happens with importmaps and module scripts. For example, 

```html
<script type="module">
  const foo = import('foo'); // not mapped, fails.
  // inject importmap script that maps foo
  const foo = import('foo'); // mapped, works...
</script>
```

>  you could get race conditions 

If there's ordering, then it seems like the fetching resource (e.g. owning link or style) needs to bake a copy of the importmap to use for any fetches it spawns. Seems like that would avoid a race and be straightfoward to reason about. I hope that's practical.

> If there's ordering, then it seems like the fetching resource (e.g. owning link or style) needs to bake a copy of the importmap to use for any fetches it spawns. Seems like that would avoid a race and be straightfoward to reason about. I hope that's practical.

@sorvell  - this wouldn't cover if the document's import maps change during the fetch though. It would have the stale copied version, so the race still exists.

@KurtCattiSchmidt Great questions!

> 1. Existing imports currently go through the module map and use specifiers (without any sort of prefix). Does this proposal imply that a Javascript `import foo;` and `import specifier:foo;` are equivalent for script-based specifier imports?

Yes, that’s the idea.

> 2. This is somewhat similar to `<base>`, and it might be helpful to list out differences or pro's/cons so it doesn't get confused or sidetracked. It also might help to describe how this is expected to work with `<base>` (I assume specifiers ignore `<base>`, but I'm not positive, it might still apply after import map resolution).

That's an interesting connection. They are quite different: `<base>` specifies the base URL to use for all relative URLs. It does not affect specifiers, since they are not relative URLs, and it should not affect `specifier:` URLs since they would be absolute, so that is internally consistent.
It *does* apply after import map resolution (see [testcase](https://000725319.codepen.website/)) but that doesn't change with `specifier:` URLs.

> 4. Script execution has finer control over when script is executed vs parsed via `async` and `defer`, so it can wait until all content (including import maps) have been parsed before executing (if desired). HTML has no such constructs, so you could have:>

> <link rel="stylesheet" href="specifier:foo" id="first">
> <script type="importmap">

>   "imports": {
>     "foo": "styles.css"
>   }
> }
> </script>
> <link rel="stylesheet" href="specifier:foo" id="second">
> ```

> One possible solution to this kind of thing would be to introduce `async` or `defer`-like attributes for each of these, which won't scale everywhere (e.g. CSS `@import` doesn't take an attribute, so it would require updates to its grammar, and I would imagine there are other strange cases). Deferring the fetch could postpone the overall load time pretty significantly though, so maybe the ordering dependency is less bad?

It's not about resource fetching in HTML vs JS, it's about when the UA discovers the specifier.
Note that this does not work today ([testcase](https://000725319.codepen.website/async-before.html)):

```html
<script type="module" async defer>
	import "foo";
</script>
<script type="importmap">
{
	"imports": {
		"foo": "./index.js"
	}
}
</script>
```

Neither URLs nor specifiers are revisited multiple times. If the *resource* being fetched is using specifiers however, these attributes may defer its loading until after the import map has been processed. None of this changes. Yes, it does mean that any resources using specifiers would need to generally come after import maps, but that's not new.

WRT async/defer for `<link>`, `@import` etc, these are orthogonal primitives, and need to be discussed in their own proposals, some of which are:
- https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3983
- https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/1603

`specifier:` URLs may add to the motivation around them, but neither is blocking the other.

Btw CSS `@import` *can* take additional annotations (media queries, `supports()`, `layer()`), so it wouldn't be a huge lift in terms of grammar.

Note that `specifier:` URLs don't need to be restricted to CSS and JS. With this, ultimately specifiers could be used anywhere a URL can, including images, videos, import map URLs (alias specifiers to other specifiers!), `<iframe src>`, SVG `<use>`, CSS `url()` etc. I added a note to the OP in case it wasn't clear.

The CSS `@import` fetching behavior is [somewhat vaguely spec'd](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade-5/#at-import), but the actual behavior in browser engines seems to be async fetches with a synchronous ordered insertion of imported rules once each fetch completes. The async fetch of `a.css` means that fetching `specifier:foo` could fail, as it would be racing with the import map parsing.

Waiting to fetch resources until parsing completes is bad, and this would also break optimizations like the [speculative parser](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#active-speculative-html-parser). This case seems worse than the ordering dependency in 3), as it's non-deterministic.

I don't think it breaks the speculative parser, it just means these _particular_ speculative fetches cannot happen until any import maps have been parsed, which seems fine to me?

In general, this is assuming the JS behavior where undefined specifiers fail early. JS has very good reasons to handle them that way, but we are not bound by the same constraints everywhere in the platform. For independent fetches that don't affect anything else, such as CSS `@import`, there is no reason to fail eagerly if you encounter a `specifier:` URL you can't resolve, you _could_ just wait longer.

Also, we _should_ define `@import` fetching less vaguely! Would you mind opening an issue?

> WRT async/defer for <link>, @import etc, these are orthogonal primitives, and need to be discussed in their own proposals

This makes sense to me. The race condition @KurtCattiSchmidt points out exists today with importmaps and js modules. Here's a [test case](https://lit.dev/playground/#gist=dc54a3c1f6198de1e317cab97aec4afb) (try setting the timeout in barMapDelay to be > barImportDelay). 

In general, I think the best practice with importmaps is to define them early and as long as you do that, it shouldn't be an issue?

The main issue with this is that it doesn't answer the question of how you use modules from the map in those places, regardless of the import map.

e.g. let's say you don't have an import map at all, but you are using a module in `/style/theme.css`.

Right now calling `@import "/style/theme.css"` would re-fetch that URL, ignoring the module map. A `specifier:` scheme is not the right primitive for this.

I think what's needed is a map of places where modules can be reused alongside non-modules, and see what is the right way to specify that the importing happens from the module map (and referring to the import map as part of that) rather than as a regular fetch.

It could be `@import module "/style/theme.css"`.
We can go with `@import "module:/style/theme.css"` which might mean also `@import module:https://cdn.example.com/style.css"`.

When looking at the use cases - I wouldn't jump to a generic solution though it might be tempting. Including HTML modules in `<iframe src>` or SVG modules in `<use>`, or image modules in CSS `url()` sound like possible future use case but in fact bring a lot of questions and complications about mutability, that might lead us to a completely different syntax.

In light of the new "Style Module Imports via `` Elements" [explainer](https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/LinkTagModuleImport/explainer.md) ... I think only a small set of HTML attributes would actually benefit from SpecifierOrURL handling, and for those I think a new attribute, say `importfrom`, is worth considering over a protocol. ```html ``` Of the 14 URL-bearing attributes in 27 HTML elements (please expand and check my list and reasoning below), and excluding ~13 additional obsolete attributes, really only `` and plausibly ~2-3 others are good candidates. This comment doesn't address CSS or SVG. I note that during the original design of import map, an `import:` scheme was [proposed](https://github.com/WICG/import-maps/blob/93f94c6dfb268bde3009644b65580fb2fbb98fcf/README.md#import-urls) in [2018](https://github.com/WICG/import-maps/issues/23#issuecomment-435511283), [scaled back to only CSS and HTML](https://github.com/WICG/import-maps/issues/75#issuecomment-440010410), and ultimately [dropped in 2021](https://github.com/WICG/import-maps/commit/c1fe41aae1c4aa5b8918b41224f83679f68d8d5b). What was not considered then, and I think should be now, is a new attribute like `importfrom`. An `importfrom` attribute offers distinct advantages over a protocol: - it offers a progressive enhancement strategy - it avoids a hard fail on non-supporting browsers (`href="specifier:foo"` results in a network error, see [scheme fetch](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#scheme-fetch)) - it avoids repurposing existing attributes to subtly-new semantics, which is discouraged by Web Platform Design Principle [Re-use HTML attribute names (only) for similar functionality](https://www.w3.org/TR/design-principles/#attribute-reuse) - it is named after its semantics, see [Name URL-containing attributes based on their primary purpose](https://www.w3.org/TR/design-principles/#naming-of-url-attributes) In the specific case of "Style Module Imports via `` Elements": - it avoids a confusing repurposing of `type` to `type="module"` - it avoids making `href` a dual-purpose attribute which triggers different behaviors of the link element itself, which is confusing and error-prone I note the design principle above already names overloading `href` as a mistake not to repeat: > **Note:** HTML has a number of legacy inconsistencies that should not be emulated, like the way `link`'s `href` attribute might allow for navigation or for resource loading, depending on the value of the element's `rel` attribute. SpecifierOrURL processing rule: If `importfrom` is present and supported, it wins and `href` is ignored. - browser without support: ignores the unknown attribute, uses `href`, loads a working stylesheet. No error, no console noise - browser with support: resolves `importfrom` through the import map, ignores `href`
Elements with URL attributes and reasoning I examined the [WHATWG HTML attributes index](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/indices.html) and cross-checked for example against the spec's own [parse a URL](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/urls-and-fetching.html#parse-a-url) call sites, and against Gecko's URL-attribute table, a literal array, [`kURLAttributesHTML`](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/source/dom/base/nsTreeSanitizer.cpp). Filtering the attributes index on the string "URL" alone is not enough. `srcset` and `` have URLs in a larger syntax and don't declare "URL" as their value type. I found 14 URL-bearing attributes, across 27 elements: - `href`: ``, `` (navigate on activation), `` (behaviour depends on `rel`), `` (sets the document base URL) - `src`: ``, `
@robglidden if we have `<link rel=stylesheet type=module>`, what is the advantage of having either `specifier:` or `importfrom`? Where would you use this outside of importing stylesheets?

Ah ok for progressive enhancement we could do that or:

link rel="stylesheet module"

Which would ignore "module" on unsupported browsers without introducing a new attribute.

The thing is that it will still fail on unsupported browsers if using module specifiers from the importmap, which makes me think that it's perhaps better for it to fail rather than sometimes succeed and sometimes fail... But I am not sure.

I think we need to distinguish import-as-module (make a resource part of the module graph) vs specifier import.
Importing a URL as a module does not automatically allow us to use specifiers, and last I checked Style Module Imports did not account for specifiers at all.
Specifiers are _essential_ for proper dependency management on the web platform. They decouple a dependency from…
- the location of its package (CDN, local, etc)
- its exact file path _within_ the package
- its exact version in the current context

Even a `<script>` element, which already supports `type=module`, does not actually support specifiers.
And there are many use cases for importing non-JS assets, from CSS libraries to icons, graphics, media files, etc. for which the web platform currently has no good story.
Sure, we could introduce ad hoc syntax for every single case. And then more ad hoc syntax in CSS, and more ad hoc syntax in SVG, and so on. This is exactly what this proposal aims to avoid. The more special syntax we add, the more the API surface authors have to learn, and the slower the rate of progress because everything now requires a bikeshedding session .
Or we can target the one syntax all of these understand: URLs.

This does not negate the value of supporting `type=module` on certain resources to add a (regular) URL to the module graph. These are separate things.

> I think we need to distinguish import-as-module (make a resource part of the module graph) vs specifier import. Importing a URL as a module does not automatically allow us to use specifiers

The main point is that importing from the specifier map means that the resource is imported from the module graph.
In what cases does importing from the module graph doesn't go through the `importmap`?

> and last I checked Style Module Imports did not account for specifiers at all.

I think it does?
`import sheet from "theme-styles" with { type: "css" }` should check the import map for a `theme-styles` specifier.

> Even a `<script>` element, which already supports `type=module`, does not actually support specifiers. 

Can you expand on that? specifiers are part of an importmap and are supported whenever a module import is supported (not to be confused with CSS `@import` unfortunately).

The more special syntax we add, the more the API surface authors have to learn, and the slower the rate of progress because everything now requires a bikeshedding session . Or we can target the one syntax all of these understand: URLs.

We would need ad-hoc understanding of what importing from the module graph means in all these cases... what does it mean for SVG to import from the module graph?
A `specifier` URL doesn't solve anything in that regard... if at some points certain parts of SVG fetch via the module graph, they should also resolve URLs using the importmap.

The importmap is nothing but a glorified URL alias system for the module graph... A custom scheme is the wrong abstraction for that IMO as it's not valid anywhere outside the module graph and it always needs to be consulted with when importing from the module graph anyway.

@noamr 

`<script src="foo" type="module"></script>` will not use a `foo` specifier: `foo` in that context already has a defined meaning, it's a relative URL to the file called `foo`. Try it. 🙂

**That is literally the whole point of this proposal.** You cannot retrofit specifiers in places designed for URLs, because they are already interpreted as relative URLs and we cannot change that. No wonder you reached the conclusion that there is no point if there's such a fundamental misunderstanding.

Last I checked style module imports were also framed around URLs, including plain relative URLs, which preclude specifiers from _ever_ being supported in these places.
By style module imports I'm not referring to CSS modules, I'm referring to the new `<link rel=stylesheet import="foo.css">` proposal. 
ESM imports avoided this entire problem by not allowing these: a relative URL has to start with `./` or `../`.

Specifiers are indeed an abstraction over URLs — an **essential** one for dependency management. The reason people use specifiers is not because they look a little prettier. It's because they decouple a dependency from:
- the exact location of the package
- the exact file path within the package (which often changes between versions)
- the exact version, for the source referencing
- the import conditions (e.g. browser, node, typescript, etc)

Worse, lack of specifiers rules out transitive dependencies because there's nothing reasonable _to_ reference. 

Specifiers are not a nice-to-have. 
Until we can use specifiers everywhere a dependency may be useful, the web platform is bound to depend on bundlers forever for dependencies (and still have "dependency management" come [3rd as a pain point](https://2025.stateofjs.com/en-US/usage/#top_js_pain_points)). You may think this is fine, but we should all be aware of what future we are designing for the web platform.

Perhaps the mistake of this proposal was coupling `specifier:` with the module graph. They can be entirely separate. It's a bit of a missed opportunity, but it does alleviate the core pain points this proposal was designed to address.
